vignette:
Michael is twenty-five years old. He works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel, a job he has held for three years. He is single, lives alone in a small apartment, and keeps to himself. He doesn’t talk much about his childhood, and when asked, he says it was “fine”—but the word comes out flat, like it belongs to someone else.

He remembers being seven years old, standing at the kitchen sink. The soap was too bubbly, and his father—his primary caregiver after his mother left—yelled that he was wasting it. The first slap came fast, the kind that doesn’t feel real until the sting settles in. After that, there was always a reason: a dish left in the sink, a shirt not folded correctly, a noise at dinner. The belt. The wooden spoon. The back of a hand. By the time he was twelve, he had learned to read his father’s moods the way a tracker reads the weather: the tightening jaw, the sudden quiet, the way a beer can was set down harder than usual.

Michael ran his house like a boot camp. He cleaned everything—floors, counters, baseboards—before his father came home from work. He learned to make himself small, silent, invisible. But it was never enough.

Now, in the present, Michael’s body still remembers. His daily life is organized around the expectation of punishment, even though no one is coming. When a guest at the hotel complains about a wrinkled bedsheet, Michael feels his chest go tight. He apologizes quickly, sometimes twice, and his hands shake as he smooths the fabric. His supervisor once touched his shoulder to get his attention; Michael flinched so hard he dropped a tray of toiletries. He said he was sorry for that too.

At work, housekeeping is a survival strategy. Michael checks each room methodically, three times over: once for dust, once for order, once for anything he might have missed. If a pillow is out of place, he resets the whole bed. He cannot leave a room until it feels *right*—until the feeling of something about to go wrong subsides. It rarely does. His coworkers think he is obsessive, maybe anxious. They don’t know that he is still trying to make himself safe.

At night, he has trouble sleeping. He checks the locks on his apartment door three times. He lies awake listening for footsteps, for the sound of a heavy hand against wood. Sometimes he dreams of the kitchen sink. The bubbles. The sting. He wakes up in a cold sweat, his palm pressed against his own face, as if he could push the memory back into his skull.

He avoids certain things without thinking: the smell of beer, the sound of a belt buckle, the way a particular tone of voice drops low before an explosion. He does not date. He does not let people get close. He once walked out of a grocery store because a toddler screamed too loudly, and his throat closed.

His apartment is clean—almost sterile. He keeps the counters clear, the floors swept. He owns few things. When a friend from work tried to give him a houseplant, he said no, because it would mean something else to manage, something that might die if he wasn’t careful enough.

Michael does not think of himself as a victim. He thinks of himself as someone who has learned to handle things. But his hands are raw from scrubbing; his back aches from the same hunched posture he held as a child. He is always waiting. For the slap. For the mistake. For the safety that never seems to arrive.
